newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Crew on Mir may wait weeks to fix oxygen systems.
newsitem.headline: Crew on Mir may wait weeks to fix oxygen systems.

text.p: The crew on the damaged Mir space station may have to wait until late September to repair its main oxygen system as a plan to repower a back-up system has failed so far, Russian space officials said on Monday.
The news was a latest in a series of setbacks for Mir, which has been running on partial power since a collision with its resupply ship on June 25 in the worst accident of its history.
In the meantime, the crew, bolstered from three members to five during a week-long handover period, is relying on a 70-day supply of oxygen "candles", officials said.

Ten days of efforts have failed to repair the main Elektron oxygen generating system in the Kvant-1 module, and experts now believe new parts from Earth may be needed, the head of Mission Control's analysis team, Yury Antoshechkin, told Reuters.

"We expected the flaw to be in the replaceable parts of the system. Then it would have been easier because we have practically all the changeable parts on board," he said. "But the main pipe and the vacuum valve, that's another problem."

On Monday engineers at Mission Control were devising ways to try to clear a blocked pipe, a procedure that would not require new parts. But it may be weeks before the crew tries out this operation, which is potentially risky as part of the Elektron pipe is welded to the space station's shell.
"Since we don't understand the dangers of this method, we are not yet planning such work," Antoshechkin said.
"If there are any doubts that need to worked out with the crew, most likely it will be after September 3, although if we do see no great danger it could be sooner."
A plan to run an extension cord to a back-up Elektron in Kvant-2, which is turned off to save energy, has also not worked because the crew lacks the proper cable, Antoshechkin said.

"If we cannot clean out the main pipe with simple solutions not requiring special parts, then both Elektron systems in the Kvant-1 and Kvant-2 modules will work only after the Shuttle arrives (in late September)," he said.

On board Mir on Monday, the old crew of commander Vasily Tsibliyev, who had developed heart problems during his mission, and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin continued an exercise programme to prepare for their return to Earth on August 14 after half year in space, a Mission Control spokesman said.

They also received a summary of recent world news, another official said, but it was not clear if it included President Boris Yeltsin's remarks on Friday which suggested the crew was at fault for Mir's recent woes.
Along with the Elektron problems, a series of even more difficult repairs await the new crew that arrived last week.
On August 20 commander Anatoly Solovyov and engineer Pavel Vinogradov will don spacesuits inside Mir and open the hatch to the dark, airless Spektr module to reconnect its solar panels.
Then on September 3, two cosmonauts -- Solovyov with Vinogradov or NASA astronaut Michael Foale -- will make a spacewalk to inspect a puncture into Spektr's exterior.
If the August 20 proceedure succeeds, then the ship should have enough energy to repower the Kvant-2 module and turn on its back-up Elektron system around August 24-25, Antoshechkin said.

A day after the old crew leaves on Thursday, the new crew will fly their escape Soyuz capsule to another docking port on the other side of Mir and take photographs of the Spektr's damaged exterior en route.
